title: Freshness signal: refresh cached data only when the source actually changes
text:
## Summary

Let a cached data source declare a cheap "has the source changed?" probe, so
Streamlit re-runs the expensive query (and updates dependent fragments) **only
when the underlying data actually changed** — instead of on a blind timer. This
is the event-driven counterpart to timer-based refresh.

## Why?

Timer-based refresh (`@st.fragment(run_every=…)`, or a server-side scheduled
refresh) fires on a fixed clock regardless of whether anything changed. For an
expensive query that forces a bad tradeoff:

- **Poll fast** → the heavy query re-runs every interval even when the data is
  identical, wasting warehouse/API cost.
- **Poll slow** → users stare at stale data between ticks.

Sources usually expose something *cheap* that reveals whether they changed — a
version token, an ETag, a `MAX(updated_at)`, a Snowflake stream or
change-tracking timestamp. There's no built-in way to poll that cheap signal
often and re-run the expensive work only when it moves.

## How?

Attach a cheap freshness function to a cached data source. Streamlit checks the
freshness token; when it changes, it invalidates the cache and re-runs the
fragments that read it. When it's unchanged, the cached value is served and no
expensive work runs.

Sketch (names illustrative):

```python
def orders_version():
    # Cheap probe — cache invalidates when this value changes.
    return conn.query("SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM orders")

@st.cache_data(freshness=orders_version)
def load_orders():
    return conn.query("SELECT * FROM orders")   # expensive; runs only on change

@st.fragment(run_every="5s")
def orders_panel():
    df = load_orders()      # cheap probe each poll; heavy query only when changed
    st.line_chart(df, x="ts", y="orders")

orders_panel()
```

title: `st.dataframe` toolbar buttons are 22.4px, below the WCAG 2.2 24px minimum target size (axe `target-size`)
text:
### Checklist
- [x] I have searched the existing issues for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary
The hover toolbar that `st.dataframe` draws (Show/hide columns, Download as CSV, Search, Fullscreen)
renders each button at 22.4 x 22.4 CSS px, and the buttons sit next to each other, so axe-core's
`target-size` rule (impact: serious, WCAG 2.2 AA, SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)) fails. Cause:
`StyledElementToolbarButton` in `frontend/lib/src/components/shared/BaseButton/styled-components.ts`
(1.64.0, line ~524) sets `padding: theme.spacing.twoXS` and `minHeight: "unset"` around a small icon.

### Reproducible Code Example
Same app as above (the `st.dataframe` line is enough).

### Steps To Reproduce
1. `streamlit run app.py`
2. Hover the dataframe so the toolbar appears.
3. Run axe-core 4.13 with the `wcag22aa` tag.

### Expected Behavior
Each toolbar button is at least 24 x 24 CSS px (or spaced so a 24px circle around each does not overlap
another target).

### Current Behavior
```
target-size (serious, wcag22aa, wcag258) — 4 nodes
<button kind="elementToolbar" data-testid="stBaseButton-elementToolbar" aria-label="Show/hide columns" class="st-emotion-cache-18ac3gt eqzt73c20">
  Target has insufficient size (22.4px by 22.4px, should be at least 24px by 24px)
<button ... aria-label="Download as CSV" ...>   (same)
<button ... aria-label="Search" ...>            (same)
<button ... aria-label="Fullscreen" ...>        (same)
```

### Suggested fix
Give `StyledElementToolbarButton` `minWidth: "1.5rem"` and `minHeight: "1.5rem"` (24px) instead of
`minHeight: "unset"`, or raise the padding one step. The toolbar is already an overlay above the element,
so the extra 1.6px per button does not move page layout. The same styled button is used by other element
toolbars (charts, `st.data_editor`), which would all pass with the one change.

In the same minimal app, axe also reports `target-size` on the `st.date_input` month/day spinbutton
segments (17.9 x 19.6px); that may deserve its own look but is secondary.

### Is this a regression?
- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.
- [x] No.

### Debug info
- Streamlit version: 1.64.0 (latest)
- Python version: 3.12
- OS: Linux (CI) and Windows 11
- Browser: Chromium (Playwright bundled)
- axe-core: 4.13.0

title: Periodic server-driven data refresh shared across sessions (vs. per-session run_every)
text:
## Summary

Provide a way to refresh a data source on a **server-side schedule** — computed
once for the whole app and pushed to every session currently viewing it —
instead of each session running its own `run_every` timer and recomputing the
same query independently. This is the shared "the dashboard refreshes every
minute and everyone sees the latest" pattern that live/ops dashboards need.

## Why?

`@st.fragment(run_every=…)` already gives time-driven updates, but the timer and
the computation are **per session**: with _N_ viewers on the same dashboard you
get _N_ timers and _N_ executions of the same query every interval. A refresh
that is cheap for one user becomes _N×_ load on the warehouse/API for a shared
internal tool.

`@st.cache_data` dedupes the *computation* across sessions, but nothing *drives*
a periodic refresh or *wakes* the sessions when a new value lands — today
`run_every` is the driver, and it's per session. The missing piece is a refresh
that runs once for the whole app and updates every session viewing it.

## How?

Mark a cached data source to refresh on a fixed interval, centrally for the
whole app. Any fragment that reads it shows the current value and re-renders when
a new one lands.

Sketch (names illustrative):

```python
# The value refreshes centrally every 60s; sessions read the current value and
# rerun when a new one lands — no per-session timer, one shared computation.
@st.cache_data(refresh_every="60s")
def latest_metrics():
    return run_warehouse_query()

@st.fragment
def kpis():
    df = latest_metrics()          # returns the current cached value immediately
    st.metric("Orders", len(df))
    st.line_chart(df, x="ts", y="orders")

kpis()
```

## Additional Context

- Split out from [#12980](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12980)
  ("real-time chart updates without rerunning the entire script"), which is being
  closed now that fragments (`run_every`), `st.rerun(scope=…)`, and element
  diffing cover the original per-session/live-update and flicker concerns.
- Related in-flight work: the non-blocking background execution spec
  ([#17067](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17067)) covers shared,
  off-thread cached computation; scheduled/recurring refresh is called out there
  as not-yet-built.
- Companion gap: a **freshness signal**
  ([#17141](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17141)) — a cheap "did
  the source change?" probe (e.g. Snowflake change-tracking / `LAST_ALTERED` /
  `MAX(updated_at)`) to drive **event-driven** invalidation instead of a blind
  timer. That's the push counterpart to this timer-based one.

title: Add `max_stale` parameter to `refresh_mode="background"` for configurable stale grace window
text:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the existing issues for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

When using `refresh_mode="background"` on `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource`, the stale grace window is fixed at 1×TTL (hard expiry at 2×TTL). This means an app idle overnight (longer than 2×TTL) has its cache evicted and the first morning user blocks on a cold miss.

A `max_stale` parameter would let users configure the stale grace window independently from TTL:

```python
@st.cache_data(ttl="2m", max_stale="12h", refresh_mode="background")
def load_data():
    return expensive_query()
```

This separates two concerns: **how often to refresh** (`ttl="2m"`) from **how long stale data is acceptable** (`max_stale="12h"`). Users who want frequent freshness checks but never want to block get exactly that.

### Why?

From [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050) (comment by @itsToggle):

> Is there any way that we can influence the "2 × ttl" background cache timeout? In my use case I want a short ttl so the values are updated often, but I never want my users to have to wait for a response. I would like to set the ttl to something like 2 minutes, but the oldest background cache that's allowed to be served can be much older than four minutes.

This is also the more practical solution for the "first user of the day" problem compared to cron scheduling, since it does not require an always-on server and works on scale-to-zero deployments.

### How?

The [background refresh spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-04-08-cache-background-refresh/product-spec.md) already calls this out as future work:

> **`max_stale` parameter**: Explicitly configure the stale grace window (default: equal to `ttl`), e.g. `ttl="1h", max_stale="12h"` to serve stale data across an overnight idle gap without blocking the first morning user

### Additional Context

- Related (closed): [#5871](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5871), [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050)

title: Add `max_stale` parameter to `refresh_mode="background"` for configurable stale grace window
text: Related aspect: you can configure the stale period via `runner.cacheBackgroundRefreshTTLMultiplier` across the entire app, but not per cache function.

title: st.user is empty in apps that use an external host auth token, because the token shares a subprotocol slot with XSRF
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

The frontend sends either a host auth token or the XSRF cookie in one `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` entry, and the host auth token wins when both exist. Because of that, an app that receives an external auth token from its host page cannot also send the XSRF token. The server cannot validate the token for those handshakes, so it does not read the signed user cookie and `st.user` stays empty.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

st.write(st.user)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Serve the app to a host page that sets `useExternalAuthToken: true` in `/_stcore/host-config`.
2. Configure an `[auth]` section so the app can sign a user in.
3. Leave `server.enableXsrfProtection` at its default value of `true`.
4. Sign in and let the host page pass its auth token to the app.
5. Read `st.user` in the app and see that it holds no user fields.

### Expected Behavior

An app should be able to send both the host auth token and the XSRF token on the handshake, so host-auth deployments get user identity without turning XSRF protection off.

### Current Behavior

`WebsocketConnection.getSessionTokens` builds the second subprotocol entry as `hostAuthToken ?? xsrfCookie ?? "PLACEHOLDER_AUTH_TOKEN"`. The server reads that one entry as the XSRF token (`_parse_subprotocols` in `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_websocket.py`). A host auth token in that slot fails `validate_xsrf_token`, so the handler skips the signed user cookie.

The handshake itself still succeeds, because an embed is same-origin and XSRF admission only applies to cross-origin handshakes. Only identity is affected.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.61.1 and `develop`
- Python version: 3.12
- Operating System: Any
- Browser: Any

### Additional Information

Split out of #16476, which made the XSRF token admission control for cross-origin WebSocket handshakes. That change documents this limitation in the `server.enableXsrfProtection` help text. Options worth weighing: carry both tokens in distinct subprotocol entries, or validate the host auth token on a separate path.

title: st.user is empty in apps that use an external host auth token, because the token shares a subprotocol slot with XSRF
text:
One more deployment shape that the shared slot affects, found while reviewing #16476.

A reverse proxy that forwards without `proxy_set_header Host $host` gives Streamlit a `Host` value such as `127.0.0.1:8501`, while the browser still sends the real page origin in `Origin`. Streamlit compares `Origin` against the `Host` header, so it treats that handshake as cross-origin even though the browser considers it same-origin.

A plain app still connects there, because its page can read the XSRF cookie and fill the token slot. An app that uses `useExternalAuthToken` cannot, because the host auth token occupies the slot the XSRF token needs. After #16476 that handshake is rejected with code `1008` rather than connecting anonymously.

Two ways to fix it, both inside the scope of this issue:

1. Carry the host auth token and the XSRF token in separate `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` entries, which fixes the identity gap and this rejection together.
2. Accept `browser.serverAddress` as an additional same-origin signal, so a proxy that hides the public host does not turn same-origin traffic into cross-origin traffic. That is operator-configured, so it does not trust `X-Forwarded-Host`.

title: Security: Add configurable WebSocket Origin allow-list
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Our enterprise application uses Streamlit WebSockets for application communication.

During an enterprise DAST/security assessment, the scanner tested the WebSocket Origin validation by modifying the Origin header to an unauthorized domain.

The WebSocket connection was still accepted.

For example, the legitimate request contains an approved Origin:

Origin: https://<approved-application-domain>

The DAST scanner changes this to:

Origin: https://malicious-example.com

The WebSocket connection is still established.

## Security Concern

Without strict Origin validation, an authenticated WebSocket connection may potentially be initiated from an unauthorized website.

This creates a security concern for enterprise applications where access is restricted to specific trusted domains.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python

```

### Steps To Reproduce

_No response_

### Expected Behavior

Streamlit should provide a supported configuration option to define an explicit WebSocket Origin allow-list.

For example:

server.websocketAllowedOrigins = [
    "https://<approved-domain>"
]

or an equivalent configuration.

The application should reject the WebSocket upgrade when the Origin is not present in the configured allow-list.

### Current Behavior

Missing WebSocket Origin Validation

Test performed by DAST:

1. Establish normal WebSocket connection.
2. Modify the Origin header to another domain.
3. Send the WebSocket upgrade request.
4. Connection is still accepted.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit: 1.60.0
- Python: 3.12
- Deployment: Azure App Service (Linux)
- Reverse proxy: Azure Application Gateway WAF v2
- Authentication: OKTA OIDC
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

Does Streamlit currently provide a supported configuration for strict WebSocket Origin validation?

If not, could a configurable WebSocket Origin allow-list be added?

This capability is required for enterprise security/DAST compliance.

title: Deprecate the `persist` option of `st.cache_data` in favor of configurable cache storage
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Deprecate the [`persist` parameter of `st.cache_data`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.cache_data) (`persist="disk"`). It doesn't fit well with the rest of the API and is incompatible with more recent features. A better, more flexible alternative is to make the **cache storage backend configurable** (e.g. via `st.App`), so users can plug in a storage that persists to disk — or Redis/S3 — consistently across the whole app.

### Why?

`persist="disk"` is a narrow, awkward escape hatch:
- It only supports a single hardcoded mode (`"disk"`) with a non-configurable location (#3018).
- It doesn't compose cleanly with other cache features — e.g. it ignores `ttl` (#4859).
- It's a per-function flag for what is really a deployment/storage concern, so it's easy to misuse and inconsistent across an app.
- It doesn't scale to multi-instance deployments (each replica has its own local disk), where users actually want a shared/central store.

A configurable storage backend addresses all of this in one coherent mechanism, and persistence becomes just one storage implementation rather than a special-cased parameter.

### How?

- **Introduce a configurable cache storage API** (per the [custom storage API spec, PR #14902](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14902)) — e.g. a `cache_storage_manager` parameter on `st.App` — that lets users supply a custom backend (disk, Redis, S3, …) applied consistently to `st.cache_data`.
  - A built-in/example disk-persisting storage would cover today's `persist="disk"` use case (with configurable location, and without the `ttl` incompatibility).
- **Deprecate `persist`** on `st.cache_data` with a long, clearly-communicated window and a documented migration path (it keeps working during deprecation). Follow "Graceful Evolution" — 3+ months notice, clear migration guidance.

### Additional Context

- Docs: [`st.cache_data`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.cache_data).
- Replacement direction: [PR #14902 — custom storage API for `st.App`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14902) (also motivated by #5849 "bring your own Redis cache").
- Related persist limitations: #4859 (`persist='disk'` ignores `ttl`), #3018 (configurable location for persistent cache).

title: Preserve coroutine-function detection for async cached functions
text:
## Summary

PR [#16168](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16168) adds async-aware `st.cache_data` and `st.cache_resource`. An async cached function remains awaitable, but the decorated object is a `CachedFunc` whose `__call__` is synchronous and returns an awaitable. As a result:

```python
import inspect

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data
async def cached_lookup(query: str) -> str:
    return await search_service(query)


assert not inspect.iscoroutinefunction(cached_lookup)
result = cached_lookup("streamlit")
assert inspect.isawaitable(result)
value = await result
```

This issue is a searchable decision record and a place to collect demand for preserving coroutine-function detection through the cache decorators. It is not committed follow-up work and does not block #16168.

## Affected integrations

Some frameworks inspect a callback before invoking it to decide whether to use their sync or async execution path:

- LangChain `RunnableLambda`
- LlamaIndex `FunctionTool`
- MCP callback/tool registration, including decorator-based tool APIs
- Similar callback systems such as Gradio

When the decorated `CachedFunc` is classified as synchronous, a framework may invoke it on its sync path and treat the returned coroutine as the sync result instead of awaiting it.

## Supported compatibility pattern

Keep the cached implementation separate and pass a true `async def` adapter to APIs that inspect callbacks. This reusable adapter preserves coroutine-function detection while still calling through the cache:

```python
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from typing import ParamSpec, TypeVar

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")


def as_async_callback(
    cached_func: Callable[P, Awaitable[R]],
) -> Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]:
    async def callback(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        return await cached_func(*args, **kwargs)

    return callback


retrieve_callback = as_async_callback(cached_lookup)

runnable = RunnableLambda(retrieve_callback)
tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=retrieve_callback)
```

For decorator-based MCP registration, keep the cached function separate from the registered tool:

```python
@st.cache_data
async def cached_customer(customer_id: int) -> dict:
    return await database.fetch(customer_id)


@mcp.tool()
async def lookup_customer(customer_id: int) -> dict:
    return await cached_customer(customer_id)
```

Do not use `inspect.unwrap(cached_lookup)` as the callback. It returns the original function and therefore bypasses Streamlit caching.

## Demand collection

Please comment if the async-adapter pattern cannot satisfy your use case. Include:

- the framework and version;
- how the callback is registered and invoked; and
- why a separate `async def` adapter is insufficient.

That evidence can inform whether Streamlit should preserve coroutine-function detection directly in a future change.

## Related

- [#16168](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16168) — async-aware cache decorators
- [#8308](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8308) — general async cached-function support

title: [feature] Add copy="cow" option to st.cache_data
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add an opt-in `copy="cow"` mode to `st.cache_data` that uses copy-on-write semantics for cached return values. This avoids unnecessary full-object deserialization on cache hits while preserving isolation between callers, significantly reducing cache-hit latency and memory allocation for large cached objects.

### Why?

`st.cache_data` currently creates an independent copy of the cached value for each call. This provides isolation between callers, but for large objects such as Pandas DataFrames and NumPy arrays, repeatedly deserializing and copying cached values can introduce significant CPU time and memory allocation overhead.

This becomes particularly relevant for applications where large datasets are read repeatedly across multiple sessions, while mutations to returned values are relatively uncommon.

An opt-in copy-on-write mode can preserve the isolation guarantees of `st.cache_data` while avoiding unnecessary full-object duplication on cache hits. The existing behavior would remain unchanged for applications that do not opt into the new mode.

In benchmarks using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0, the prototype reduced observed cache-hit latency by approximately 2.7–3.2× for DataFrames ranging from 5,000 to 1,000,000 rows. In a separate allocation benchmark with 10 consecutive reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB to 0.02–0.03 MB.

### How?

Introduce an optional `copy` parameter on `st.cache_data`:

```python
@st.cache_data(copy="cow")
def load_data():
    return pd.read_parquet("large_dataset.parquet")

### Additional Context

### Prototype

A working prototype is available in my fork:

https://github.com/Isllanrx/streamlit/tree/feature/cache-data-cow

The implementation is currently limited to the following areas:

- `st.cache_data` API support for `copy="cow"`
- Copy-on-write handling for supported cached return values
- Caller/session mutation isolation
- Integration with existing cache lifecycle and eviction behavior
- Unit tests for mutation isolation
- Static typing coverage for the public API

### Performance Benchmark

The prototype was benchmarked using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0.

| Dataset | Default copy | `copy="cow"` | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 × 12 | 0.155 ms | 0.055 ms | 2.8× |
| 50,000 × 12 | 0.158 ms | 0.049 ms | 3.2× |
| 200,000 × 12 | 0.144 ms | 0.048 ms | 3.0× |
| 1,000,000 × 12 | 0.131 ms | 0.049 ms | 2.7× |

In a separate allocation benchmark using 10 consecutive cache reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB with the existing behavior to approximately 0.02–0.03 MB with `copy="cow"`.

### Stress Testing

The implementation was also tested under concurrent mutation and cache lifecycle pressure:

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 50 concurrent threads mutating the same 100,000-row DataFrame | Passed |
| Nested dictionaries containing DataFrames, Series, and lists | Passed |
| 200 concurrent cache entries with `max_entries=5` | Passed |
| Concurrent readers while repeatedly calling `.clear()` | Passed |
| 1,000,000-row (~100 MB) DataFrame with mutation isolation | Passed |

The concurrent mutation test completed in approximately 0.046 seconds. The cached DataFrame remained unchanged and no cross-caller mutations were observed.

The 1,000,000-row test also preserved mutation isolation, with subsequent reads completing in approximately 0.08 ms.

These tests were specifically designed to validate both the performance characteristics and the isolation guarantees of the proposed copy-on-write behavior.

The application uses SQL Server 2017 through pyodbc and processes relatively large datasets with st.cache_data. Because each cache hit can involve deserialization and additional memory allocation, memory usage can increase significantly under concurrent sessions. In our Kubernetes environment, this has repeatedly caused pods to exceed their memory limits and get OOM-killed.

I built this prototype based on that real-world workload. With copy="cow", repeated reads can reuse the cached object’s underlying data while still isolating mutations between callers, which resulted in a significant reduction in memory allocation in my benchmarks.

title: [feature] Add copy="cow" option to st.cache_data
text:
@sfc-gh-lwilby-1  To give you more concrete context, this proposal came directly from a production workload where we were hitting this limitation in practice.

### 1. Production Architecture & The Memory Bottleneck

We run an enterprise indicators and metrics application on Kubernetes, with pods limited to **2 vCPU and 4 GB of RAM**. The application reads data from **SQL Server 2017 via `pyodbc`**, as well as a hybrid historical data lake containing hundreds of monthly Parquet files.

Under concurrent usage, the default `st.cache_data` behavior became a significant memory bottleneck. On cache hits, cached values are deserialized for each caller, so multiple concurrent sessions reading the same large DataFrame can result in multiple in-memory copies of essentially the same data.

With approximately **10–50 concurrent users**, some of our cached DataFrames were in the **15–70 MB** range uncompressed. Under load, process RSS could grow to approximately **3.0–3.9 GB**, eventually causing Kubernetes to terminate the pod with **OOMKilled (exit 137)**.

### 2. The Rust Experiment

Before working on `copy="cow"`, I also built a native Rust component (`indicadores_core`) using **PyO3**, `pyo3-arrow`, and Arrow/Parquet to optimize the cold path for historical data ingestion and filtering.

The Rust implementation produced meaningful improvements:

- **30–40% lower CPU time** for ingestion under Linux
- **1.4×–1.6× higher throughput** under concurrent load

However, the stress tests revealed that improving the ingestion path did not solve the main memory problem. Once the data crossed into Python, Streamlit could still create multiple copies of the same DataFrame across concurrent callers.

That led to an important finding:

> Optimizing data ingestion can reduce CPU cost and cold-path latency, but it does not address the per-caller memory duplication on `st.cache_data` cache hits.

### 3. The Copy-on-Write Approach

The next step was to introduce a process-level shared cache for the hot path and return shallow copies backed by **Pandas 3 Copy-on-Write** semantics.

For DataFrames, the implementation uses `copy(deep=False)` while also creating defensive copies of the index and columns so that metadata mutations do not leak between callers.

We then stress-tested the approach in a Linux container matching our Kubernetes limits (`2 CPUs`, `4 GB RAM`) with **50 concurrent sessions** against production-like workloads.

| Mode | Peak RSS | p95 Latency | Throughput | Pod Status |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Standard deserialize/copy | 2.67–3.92 GB | 3.3–5.8 s | 10.6–17.4 req/s | OOMKilled |
| Native Rust reader only | 3.02–3.79 GB | 2.6–4.1 s | 16.0–27.0 req/s | OOMKilled |
| CoW shared cache | **251–303 MB** | **134–221 ms** | **622–977 req/s** | **Stable, 0 OOMs** |

The most significant result was memory usage: peak RSS dropped from approximately **3.9 GB to ~270 MB**, which eliminated the OOMKills in this workload.

We also verified mutation isolation: callers could modify their returned DataFrames independently without modifying the cached baseline or affecting other callers.

### 4. Why This Led to `copy="cow"`

This exposed a gap between the two existing cache models:

- `st.cache_resource` allows objects to be shared, but callers operate on the same object and mutations are therefore shared.
- `st.cache_data` provides caller isolation, but achieves that isolation through serialization/deserialization and independent copies.

For large analytical datasets, there is a useful middle ground:

**shared underlying data + isolated caller-visible objects + copy-on-write on mutation.**

That is what `copy="cow"` is intended to provide as an **opt-in** mode, while keeping the existing `st.cache_data` behavior unchanged by default.

The prototype was built specifically from this production use case, and the reduction in memory allocation is the main reason I believe this behavior could be useful in Streamlit itself.

title: Support stable UI placement for concurrent async tasks
text:
### Summary

When independent top-level async cached functions emit `st.*` messages concurrently, users may need their relative UI placement to stay stable and the layout to be identical on cache misses and hits.

That guarantee is not currently supported. Concurrent calls can mechanically render, but coroutine scheduling controls how their messages interleave. Each cached call owns a separate replay list, and those lists cannot reconstruct the cross-call interleaving observed during the original computations.

This does **not** mean that `asyncio.gather()`, async caching, or normal `st.*` calls from one cached function are unsupported. A single cached call continues to capture and replay its messages in order. The unsupported case is deterministic relative placement across independent concurrent cached calls.

This issue is a decision record and a place to collect demand. We are unlikely to implement a new mechanism unless real use cases show that the alternatives below are insufficient.

### Pattern without an ordering guarantee

The async cache decorators in #16168 make this pattern executable:

```python
import asyncio

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data
async def load_customers() -> int:
    st.write("Loading customers")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    st.write("Customers loaded")
    return 120


@st.cache_data
async def load_revenue() -> str:
    st.write("Loading revenue")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    st.write("Revenue loaded")
    return "$1.2M"


async def main() -> None:
    await asyncio.gather(load_customers(), load_revenue())


asyncio.run(main())
```

The output order and the miss-versus-hit interleaving are not guaranteed. This is specifically a UI-placement limitation, not a limitation on using `asyncio.gather()`.

### Recommended: join before rendering

Return data from the cached functions, await them concurrently, and render sequentially in source order:

```python
import asyncio

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data
async def load_customers() -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return 120


@st.cache_data
async def load_revenue() -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return "$1.2M"


async def load_all() -> tuple[int, str]:
    customers, revenue = await asyncio.gather(load_customers(), load_revenue())
    return customers, revenue


customers, revenue = asyncio.run(load_all())
st.metric("Customers", customers)
st.metric("Revenue", revenue)
```

This provides deterministic source-order layout, at the cost of waiting for all results before rendering them.

### Recommended: reserve stable progressive sections

`@st.fragment(parallel=True)` is already available on `develop` (implemented in #15173). Each fragment reserves its own container at its call site, so sections can complete progressively without moving relative to one another. Until native async cache decorators from #16168 are available, a synchronous cached wrapper can drive each async fetch:

```python
import asyncio

import streamlit as st


async def fetch_customers() -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return 120


async def fetch_revenue() -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return "$1.2M"


@st.cache_data
def load_customers() -> int:
    return asyncio.run(fetch_customers())


@st.cache_data
def load_revenue() -> str:
    return asyncio.run(fetch_revenue())


@st.fragment(parallel=True)
def customers_section() -> None:
    st.metric("Customers", load_customers())


@st.fragment(parallel=True)
def revenue_section() -> None:
    st.metric("Revenue", load_revenue())


customers_section()
revenue_section()
```

This is the best currently available alternative when progressive rendering and stable source-order placement are both required. After #16168 lands, each fragment can instead call an async cached function through `asyncio.run()`.

Async fragment bodies are not currently justified as a distinct capability for this problem: they would mostly be syntax sugar over driving async work inside a fragment unless users identify a missing lifecycle or compatibility need.

### Feedback wanted

Please comment with concrete cases where join-before-render and independent parallel fragments do not fit, especially if you need:

- progressive results rather than waiting for the full join;
- one shared event loop or loop-bound clients;
- source-order placement versus completion-order placement; or
- behavior that independent parallel fragments cannot provide.

Please also describe why the alternatives fail and what miss/hit layout users should observe.

### Related

- #16168 — async-aware `st.cache_data` and `st.cache_resource`
- #8308 — async cache decorator feature request
- #14277 — merged parallel fragments product spec
- #15173 — parallel fragments implementation

text:

### Summary

expose_tokens ignored when using st.App(secrets=...)
I’m using Streamlit 1.59.0 with st.App(..., secrets=...) and built-in auth.

Login works, and st.secrets["auth"]["expose_tokens"] is available inside the app, but st.user.tokens.to_dict() remains empty.

**Expexted** : 
`st.user.tokens.to_dict()` should return {"access": "..."}

**Actual**:
`st.user.tokens.to_dict()` returns {}

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

app = st.App(
    script_path="main.py",
    secrets={
        "auth": {
            "redirect_uri": ".../oauth2callback",
            "cookie_secret": "...",
            "expose_tokens": ["access"],
            "okta": {
                "client_id": "...",
                "client_secret": "...",
                "server_metadata_url": "...",
            },
        }
    },
)

st.login("okta")
st.write(st.user.tokens)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

_No response_

### Expected Behavior

`st.user.tokens.to_dict()` should return {"access": "..."}

### Current Behavior

`st.user.tokens.to_dict()` returns {}

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

**Environment**:
- Streamlit 1.59.0
- Python 3.11
- Auth provider: Okta

### Additional Information

**Codex analyse** :
issue is in streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_websocket.py.
expose_tokens is read once when the WebSocket handler is created:

def create_websocket_handler(runtime):
    expose_tokens = get_expose_tokens_config()
But with st.App(secrets=...), programmatic secrets seem to be merged later during app startup/lifespan. So the handler may capture expose_tokens=[] before the injected secrets are available.

title: Add a first-party Playwright-based e2e testing API (`streamlit.testing.e2e`) alongside AppTest
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a first-party, Playwright-based **end-to-end (browser) testing API** for Streamlit apps — `streamlit.testing.e2e` — as an optional `streamlit[testing]` extra, complementing the existing browserless unit-testing API (`AppTest`). It would provide a Streamlit-aware semantic facade for finding and operating elements in a real browser, rerun/navigation-aware synchronization, useful failure artifacts, and an escape hatch to native Playwright `Page`/`Locator`. Design thoughts are in the [app testing toolkit spec (PR #16041)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16041).

### Why?

Today users face an unhelpful choice: `AppTest` is fast and Python-native but runs no real frontend (so it can disagree with a real app, and can't cover rendering, custom components, accessibility, media, charts, or real user journeys), while browser testing can validate the real product but Streamlit provides **no supported way** to start the app, wait for reruns, select elements, collect logs, or test a deployed/embedded app — users must assemble and maintain all that infrastructure. Streamlit's own mature `e2e_playwright/` suite solves these hard problems (process lifecycle, ephemeral ports, app-idle detection, traces, iframes, uploads, dataframes/charts, etc.) but is coupled to the repo layout and private DOM test IDs, so it isn't a releasable public API.

This is especially costly for **AI coding agents**, which need a deterministic run command, semantic element identity, a compact description of the current UI, and actionable failure artifacts to validate their work — indexes, private CSS/test IDs, sleeps, and screenshots alone make brittle tests.

### How?

Ship a two-layer testing story with clear boundaries (don't build a third UI-testing engine, and don't turn AppTest into a browser emulator):

- **AppTest (browserless)** stays the fast option for logic/state/basic widget workflows — with improved runtime fidelity and typed + universal semantic queries (`get_by_key`/`get_by_label`/`get_by_text`) and a compact `snapshot()`.
- **`streamlit.testing.e2e` (browser)** — the new Playwright-based API, installed via `pip install "streamlit[testing]"`.

Proposed shape (from the spec):

```python
from playwright.sync_api import expect
from streamlit.testing.e2e import StreamlitPage, app_fixture

app = app_fixture("app.py")

def test_sign_in(app: StreamlitPage):
    app.get_element_by_label("Username", type="text_input").set_value("ada")
    app.get_element_by_label("Password", type="text_input").set_value("correct horse battery staple")
    app.get_element_by_label("Sign in", type="button").click()

    welcome = app.get_element_by_text("Welcome, ada", type="heading")
    expect(welcome.locator).to_be_visible()
```

Key capabilities:
- **App lifecycle fixture:** `app_fixture()` starts one app server per test module on an ephemeral localhost port, gives an isolated browser page per test, and waits until the initial run is idle. Also target direct/external URLs (deployed/embedded apps).
- **Semantic selection:** strict, retrying finders that understand Streamlit elements and layout containers — `get_element_by_key` / `get_element_by_label` / `get_element_by_text`, plus `get_element(type=...)` / `get_elements(type=...)`; a returned element that is a container (sidebar, form, expander, popover, dialog, tab, column, container) can scope further queries. An optional `type` discriminator maps to a generated public `ElementType` taxonomy for IDE completion.
- **Rerun/navigation-aware synchronization** so tests don't rely on sleeps.
- **Actionable failure artifacts** (text/logs/traces/screenshots) and a **semantic snapshot** (`semantic_snapshot()`) as a token-efficient interface for humans and agents.
- **Escape hatch** to native Playwright `Page`/`Locator` for anything the facade doesn't cover.
- A shared **testability vocabulary** across both layers (public element types, labels, keys, containers), explicitly optimized for AI agents.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [PR #16041 — \`[spec] Streamlit app testing toolkit\`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16041) (`specs/2026-07-16-streamlit-app-testing-toolkit/product-spec.md`).
- Related: open `feature:app-testing` issues, e.g. #9786, #13163, #9128.

title: Add a link/bookmark element that renders a rich link preview card
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a link/bookmark element that renders a URL as a rich preview card — with properties like an icon/favicon, title, description, and optionally a preview image — similar to how a bookmark looks in Notion or a link result in Google search. It could optionally **auto-fetch** these properties (e.g. from the page's Open Graph / metadata) when they aren't provided explicitly, and it should **adapt its layout** based on which properties are present.

### Why?

Links are everywhere in apps (sources, references, related resources, docs), but a bare Markdown link is visually flat. A rich, consistent link/bookmark card makes references look polished and scannable — great for dashboards, research/agent apps that cite sources, resource lists, and "read more" sections. Today users hand-build these with columns + images + markdown or custom components, which is fiddly and inconsistent.

### How?

A new element, e.g.:

```python
st.link_preview(
    "https://streamlit.io",
    title="Streamlit • A faster way to build and share data apps",
    description="Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for data scientists and AI/ML engineers to deliver interactive data apps – in only a few lines of code.",
    icon="https://streamlit.io/favicon.png",   # icon/favicon
    image="https://.../preview.png",           # optional large preview image
)

# Minimal — auto-fetch metadata from the URL:
st.link_preview("https://streamlit.io")
```

Behavior:
- **Dynamic layout:** adapt the card to whichever properties are provided — e.g. compact (favicon + title + description) vs. a larger card with a preview image (like the two reference looks below).
- **Auto-fetch (optional):** when title/description/icon/image aren't given, fetch them from the target URL's metadata (Open Graph / `<meta>` / favicon). Should be opt-in-friendly and degrade gracefully if fetching fails or is blocked (fall back to just the URL/title). Consider caching and the SiS/Community-Cloud implications of server-side fetching (and whether fetching happens backend- or frontend-side).
- Whole card is a link to the URL; supports opening in a new tab.

**Alternative / complementary: a Markdown directive.** This could also be exposed as a Markdown directive so bookmarks can be embedded inline in any markdown text (e.g. `st.markdown`), for example:

```
:bookmark[https://python-markdown.github.io/extensions/toc/]{title="Foo" icon=":material/info:"}
```

The directive attributes (`title`, `description`, `icon`, `image`, …) map to the same properties as the element, and unspecified ones can be auto-fetched. A directive plays nicely with LLM-generated content and lets bookmarks appear inline within larger blocks of text.

**Simpler inline "mentions".** The same directive family could also cover a lighter-weight inline link — not a full card, but a link that doesn't use the default link color and instead has a more button-like hover effect, with a configurable icon and title. For example:

```
:mention[URL]{text="My link"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="🍀"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="github"}
:mention[URL]{icon="streamlit"}
```

This gives a compact, chip/mention-style link (great inline in text or chat) that sits between a plain Markdown link and the full bookmark card.

Reference looks (a compact link result vs. a larger card with a preview image):

- Compact: favicon + site + bold title (link color) + description snippet.
- Rich: title + description on the left, with a preview image on the right and favicon + URL at the bottom.

### Additional Context

- Inspired by link/bookmark cards in Notion and rich link results in Google search.
- Complements a possible OEmbed feature (embedding Streamlit content elsewhere); this is the inverse — richly embedding external links inside a Streamlit app.
- Related: #11990 (file chip element, e.g. for `st.chat_message`) — a similar compact, reference-style element that could share design/infrastructure.

title: Add page and app descriptions (`page_description`, `st.Page`, `st.App`)
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add first-class authored descriptions at the page and app level: `page_description` on `st.set_page_config`, optionally `description` on `st.Page`, and a static title + description on `st.App`. Today a page can declare a title and icon, and an app has no catalog-level identity at all — so SEO, assistive tech, navigation, and non-browser clients all have to infer meaning from body copy.

### Why?

A Streamlit page already has `page_title` / `title` and `page_icon` / `icon`. There is no matching place to say what the page or the app *is*. Authors stuff that into `st.caption`, `st.markdown`, or `menu_items["About"]`, none of which is structured metadata.

That gap shows up in several places that all want the same authored sentence:

- **SEO and link previews.** Search and social crawlers need a description (and today only Community Cloud injects sharing tags). Related: #16634, #6567, #2469, #9058.
- **Accessibility.** A document-level description is the page analogue of alt text (#8563 covers elements; this is the page/app layer).
- **Multipage navigation.** `st.Page` can name a page but cannot explain it, so a nav list or catalog cannot tell "Regional revenue" from "Reports" without running the page.
- **Non-browser clients.** An agent snapshot currently serializes `url_path`, `title`, and `icon` only. A static app descriptor should be able to return title + description *without executing app code* — which is why the app-level fields belong on `st.App`, not only inside the script.

### How?

**Page description on `st.set_page_config`**, matching `page_title` / `page_icon`:

```python
st.set_page_config(
    page_title="Regional revenue",
    page_icon=":material/payments:",
    page_description=(
        "Net revenue by billing region. Excludes refunds. Periods are UTC."
    ),
)
```

**Optional `description` on `st.Page`**, so the page list carries copy without running each page (consistent with `title` / `icon`, not `page_*`):

```python
st.Page(
    "revenue.py",
    title="Regional revenue",
    icon=":material/payments:",
    description="Net revenue by billing region. Excludes refunds.",
)
```

**Static title and description on `st.App`**, available without executing the script:

```python
app = st.App(
    "main.py",
    title="Finance apps",
    description=(
        "Internal finance dashboards. Net revenue excludes refunds and is in EUR."
    ),
)
```

Suggested behavior:

- `st.Page.description` is the default for that page; `st.set_page_config(page_description=...)` overrides it for the current run (same additive pattern as today's page title).
- Single-page apps that never call `st.Page` still get a description via `set_page_config`.
- `st.App` title/description are app-level and static. They do not replace per-page title/description. For `streamlit run` apps without `st.App`, the default page's title/description (or a future config option) can stand in.
- Consumers of the same strings: HTML `<meta name="description">` / Open Graph, assistive tech, navigation (if we choose to surface it), and structured snapshots / a static app descriptor.

**Naming.** `page_description` on `set_page_config` matches `page_title`. On `st.Page` and `st.App`, `description` / `title` match the existing `title` parameter (the [agent-app interface spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/docs/agent-app-interface/specs/2026-08-28-agent-app-interface/product-spec.md) also floated `app_title` / `app_description` on `st.App` if we want the prefix explicit).

**Not in this request:** element-level alternative text for images, charts, and tables (#8563) and `help` on media (#3133). Arbitrary extra `<meta>` tags (GSC verification, etc.) stay with #16634.

### Additional Context

- Suggested as a standalone follow-up in the [agent-app interface spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/docs/agent-app-interface/specs/2026-08-28-agent-app-interface/product-spec.md) ([#16843](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843), follow-up #3): apps should explain themselves in authored metadata, not only in body widgets. Worth doing on accessibility and SEO merits even without the agent interface.
- Related:
  - #16634 — inject `<meta>` tags; a first-class `page_description` is the content those tags would publish, not a general meta-tag API
  - #6567 — social sharing meta tags outside Community Cloud
  - #2469 (closed) — `st.set_page_config(description=...)`
  - #9058 — title/favicon in the initial HTML (same "available before JS" problem)
  - #8563 — element-level alt text
  - #5673 (closed) — config-file website metadata

title: st.file_uploader hangs indefinitely on small files when sentry_sdk.init() runs in-process before Streamlit starts
text:
**Summary**

File uploads under ~10KB hang indefinitely (eventually timing out client-side) when `sentry_sdk.init()` is called in the same process, before Streamlit's own event loop is created, and Streamlit is then started in that process (e.g. via `streamlit.web.cli.main()` after rewriting `sys.argv`, rather than a fresh `streamlit run` subprocess). Uploads over ~10KB are unaffected. This reproduces with no application code beyond a single `st.file_uploader()`.

This in-process launch pattern is common for wrapper entrypoints that do setup (init error tracking, run DB migrations, etc.) before starting Streamlit without spawning a new OS process.

**Reproducible Code Example**

```python
"""
pip install streamlit==1.61.1 sentry-sdk==2.61.1
python repro.py
Then open http://localhost:8501 and upload a file smaller than ~10KB.
"""
import sys
import pathlib

pathlib.Path("app.py").write_text('''
import streamlit as st
uploaded = st.file_uploader("pick a file")
if uploaded is not None:
    st.write(f"Got {uploaded.name}, {len(uploaded.getvalue())} bytes")
''')

import sentry_sdk
sentry_sdk.init(dsn=None)  # comment this line out and the hang disappears

from streamlit.web import cli
sys.argv = ["streamlit", "run", "app.py"]
sys.exit(cli.main())
```

**Steps To Reproduce**

1. `pip install streamlit==1.61.1 sentry-sdk==2.61.1`
2. Save the snippet above as `repro.py`, run `python repro.py`
3. Open `http://localhost:8501`, upload any file smaller than ~10KB (e.g. a 300-byte CSV)
4. Upload hangs indefinitely. Comment out `sentry_sdk.init(dsn=None)` and it succeeds instantly. Upload a file larger than ~10KB and it succeeds either way.

**Expected Behavior**

Upload completes regardless of file size or whether Sentry was initialized in-process before Streamlit started.

**Current Behavior**

Small uploads hang. Root-caused to Sentry's `StarletteIntegration` (enabled by default) — confirmed via `sentry_sdk.init(dsn=None, disabled_integrations=[StarletteIntegration()])` (succeeds) vs. `disabled_integrations=[ThreadingIntegration()]` (still hangs — ruling out threading despite superficial similarity to #15374 / #16139, both of which are already fixed in this version and don't apply since this repro has no `st.fragment(run_every=...)`). `StarletteIntegration` instruments Starlette's ASGI request lifecycle, and the hang lives inside Starlette's own multipart parser — Sentry wraps exactly the layer that breaks.

**Is this a regression?**

Not tested on older versions — can test if useful.

**Debug info**

- Streamlit version: 1.61.1
- Python version: 3.12
- OS: macOS (also reproduces in a Linux container)
- sentry-sdk version: 2.61.1

**Additional Information**

Fuller repro with isolation scripts (control, all-integrations-disabled, Starlette-only-disabled) and sample CSVs: https://gist.github.com/tbrambor/d41b40950a0061ca404fc0d67e4768ed

title: Exception type too broad in error handling
text:
## Bug Report

### Description
Some `except` clauses catch overly broad exception types (e.g., bare `except:` or `except Exception:`), which can accidentally swallow important errors like `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit`.

### Example
```python
# Problematic:
try:
    do_something()
except:  # catches EVERYTHING including KeyboardInterrupt
    pass

# Better:
try:
    do_something()
except ValueError as e:
    logger.warning(f"Value error: {e}")
```

### Expected Behavior
Exception handlers should catch only the specific exceptions they know how to handle.

### Impact
- Makes it impossible to interrupt the program with Ctrl+C in some cases
- Hides unexpected errors that should be investigated
- Makes debugging significantly harder

### Suggested Fix
Replace broad `except` clauses with specific exception types wherever possible.

title: Keyed `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` keep positional selection and edit state across a data change, so actions land on the wrong row
text: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues. - [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue. ### Summary A keyed `st.dataframe` or `st.data_editor` excludes its data from the element identity: `key_as_main_identity={"selection_mode", "is_selection_activated"}` at [arrow.py lines 1280-1284](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/elements/arrow.py#L1280-L1284). The element id therefore survives a data refresh, and the browser resends grid state that was computed against the previous frame. `event.selection.rows` and `edited_rows` are positional, so after a rerun that reorders or inserts rows those positions address different records, and the app receives a selection or an edit for a row the user never touched. There is no error and no warning. The comment directly above that call site acknowledges that selections "can become orphaned when the data changes" and that resetting them "might be a nice enhancement"; the effect on an app that acts on the selection is a wrong-row write, not a cosmetic orphan. ### Reproducible Code Example ```Python import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0) st.session_state.setdefault("closed", []) # Simulates a queue whose contents change between reruns (a new ticket arrived). rows = ["TICK-101", "TICK-102", "TICK-103", "TICK-104"] if st.session_state["gen"]: rows = ["TICK-100", *rows] df = pd.DataFrame({"ticket": rows}) event = st.dataframe(df, key="queue", on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") if st.button("Simulate new ticket arriving", key="refresh"): st.session_state["gen"] += 1 st.rerun() if st.button("Close selected", key="close") and event.selection.rows: position = event.selection.rows[0] st.session_state["closed"].append(df.iloc[position]["ticket"]) st.write("Selected positions:", event.selection.rows) st.write("Closed:", st.session_state["closed"]) ``` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. `streamlit run` (or `uv run streamlit run`) the snippet. 2. Click the row showing `TICK-102` (position 1). The app shows `Selected positions: [1]`. 3. Click "Simulate new ticket arriving". `TICK-102` gets bumped down to position 2, but the highlighted row and `event.selection.rows` are still `[1]`, which is now `TICK-101`. 4. Click "Close selected". You get `Closed: ['TICK-101']` even though you had initially selected `TICK-102`. The same holds for `st.data_editor` with the default `num_rows="fixed"`: a pending `edited_rows` entry is re-applied at the same position after the frame changes. The identity part can be shown without a browser, using `AppTest`: ```python from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest def script(): import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0) if st.button("refresh", key="refresh"): st.session_state["gen"] += 1 rows = ["TICK-101", "TICK-102", "TICK-103", "TICK-104"] if st.session_state["gen"]: rows = ["TICK-100", *rows] df = pd.DataFrame({"ticket": rows}) st.dataframe(df, key="queue", on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") st.dataframe(df, on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") at = AppTest.from_function(script).run() keyed, unkeyed = at.dataframe[0].proto.id, at.dataframe[1].proto.id at.button(key="refresh").click().run() print(keyed == at.dataframe[0].proto.id) # True -> keyed id survives the data change print(unkeyed == at.dataframe[1].proto.id) # False -> unkeyed id does not ``` ### Expected Behavior When the data behind a keyed grid changes, stale selection and edit state should be reset (or the state should be keyed by row identity rather than position), so an app never receives positions computed against a frame it is no longer showing. At minimum the docs for `key=` on `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` should say that selection and edit state is positional and survives data changes. ### Current Behavior Positional selection and edit state is preserved across data changes for keyed grids. Dropping `key=` makes the id data-dependent and the stale state orphans to empty, which is safe but discards every pending selection or edit on any data change, and contradicts the general advice to always give widgets a key. ### Is this a regression? - [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version. Not a recent regression, at least. The row retarget in steps 1-4 was observed in Chromium on 1.60.0. The `AppTest` demonstration above prints `True` / `False` on both 1.63.0 and 1.64.0 (the latest release at the time of writing), and the identity code is unchanged at the current tip of `develop`. On 1.60.0 and later the `st.data_editor` case is wider than on 1.59.x: a keyed editor with `num_rows="fixed"` re-applies a pending edit at the same position after a reorder, where 1.59.x discarded it. ### Debug info - Streamlit version: 1.63.0 and 1.64.0, both reproduced - Python version: 3.14.6 - Operating System: Linux Mint 22.3 Zena 64-bit - Browser: Version 152.0.7977.82 (Official Build) for Linux Mint (x86_64) ### Additional Information Related: `_apply_dataframe_edits` ([data_editor.py#L560-L564](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/data_editor.py#L560-L564)) receives no `disabled` argument, so `disabled=["_index"]` is enforced only in the browser; a client-sent index edit is applied server-side. Apps that act on grid state currently have to pin the frame they rendered in `st.session_state`, resolve positions against that frame, and reject anything they did not serve.

title: Minimize `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` errors
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Reduce how often developers hit `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` (duplicate widget/element ID) errors by making element ID generation smarter about the surrounding container context — so that identical widgets placed in different containers (chat messages, fragments, columns, etc.) don't collide without the developer having to manually craft unique `key`s everywhere.

### Why?

It's increasingly common to have repeating identical widgets across different chat messages, fragment calls, or columns. Today the developer must manage and track a unique `key` for each, which adds a lot of boilerplate and complexity. This is especially painful in chat/LLM apps (in-chat interactive widgets, code-eval "run" buttons, generated suggestion buttons) — and for LLM-generated code it can be nearly impossible to solve, since the model may emit duplicate widgets across messages. `st.form` already avoids this within forms (the `form_id` is part of the ID), which shows the approach can work more broadly.

This is a high-impact papercut: `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` is the **No. 3 most thrown uncaught exception type**, occurring in ~**0.5% of all apps**.

A related pain point: some elements raise `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` and tell you to add a `key`, but **don't actually support a `key` argument**, leaving no clean fix. Examples:
- #11424 — showing the same `st.plotly_chart` multiple times raises `StreamlitDuplicateElementId`.
- #11360 — multiple `st.audio` calls with the same parameters and `autoplay=True` raise a duplicate error that prompts you to add a key, but `st.audio` has no `key`.

### How?

Incorporate more of the container context into an element's ID computation, focusing on **stable, explicit signals** (not user-facing text). Ideas:

- **Wrapping container keys:** automatically include the `key` of wrapping containers / `st.fragment` / `st.form` (those that support keys) in the child element's ID computation. Only for containers that have an explicit key set.
  - If we do this, it strengthens the case for **adding `key` to more containers and elements** — see #9580 and the concrete cases #11424 (`st.plotly_chart`) and #11360 (`st.audio`), plus #6152.
- **Re-evaluate key namespaces and parent-key reuse:** regular element keys, form IDs, and fragment definition keys are currently tracked in separate registries. `st.form` already contributes its `form_id` to the auto-generated IDs of unkeyed children; fragment keys identify fragment definitions but are not currently part of regular child element ID computation. Consider both:
  - Reusing explicit form / fragment / keyed-container keys as stable parent context for **unkeyed** descendants.
  - Whether form and fragment keys should participate in the same duplicate-key checks as regular element keys, or remain separate namespaces that only contribute parent context.

  Treat registry unification as a compatibility decision: the same string can currently be reused between some form / fragment and regular-element keys, and one keyed fragment definition can intentionally run from multiple call sites. Preserve the rule that an explicit child `key` is authoritative and independent of its container.
- **Column index in `st.columns`:** include the column number in the ID computation so the same widget in different columns of the same `st.columns` call doesn't collide.
- **Parent container types:** include the parent container type(s) as part of the ID computation.

**Important caution — be conservative about what goes into ID generation.** Adding container context to the ID changes element identity, which has a subtle downside: a widget that **dynamically moves between containers** (e.g. its wrapping container changes across reruns) would get a new ID and thus lose its identity and state. This is the main risk to weigh (more so than existing widget state resetting on upgrade), and it can be fixed by explicitly setting a `key` on that element so its identity no longer depends on the container context. In particular:
- **Do not** include user-facing **labels/titles** of wrapping containers (e.g. expander label, dialog title, popover label, tab name) in the ID — these change often and would be fragile/surprising. Prefer **explicitly set keys** for disambiguation instead.
- Auto-added context must apply **only to widgets without an explicit `key`**. When a user sets an explicit `key="x"`, the ID must **not** include the added container context — an explicit key should always behave predictably and stay stable regardless of the surrounding containers. Think through backwards compatibility / migration carefully.

### Additional Context

- Add `key` to more elements/containers: #9580, and concrete duplicate-ID cases where no `key` is available today: #11424 (`st.plotly_chart`), #11360 (`st.audio`).
- Related: #6152 (composable/reusable component API for larger apps).
- `st.form` already includes `form_id` in widget ID generation — a useful precedent.
- There is an older internal product spec exploring options (implicit container key-prefix, adding `key`/`key_prefix` to containers, best-practice docs, or fixing duplicate IDs via enumeration). This issue intentionally leans toward the conservative, explicit-key-based approaches from that discussion.

title: Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for st.login() sessions
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add opt-in support for Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) to the native authentication flow, so the _streamlit_user cookie set by st.login() becomes useless when copied off the device it was issued on.

Currently only Chrome takes advantage of this but I am happy to implement it and open a pull request
W3C draft: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-dbsc/

### Why?

Since 1.42, st.login() stores the user's identity in a signed cookie with a 30-day lifetime. The cookie is HttpOnly and Secure, which is right, but there is no server-side session state: a cookie copied from a browser profile by malware or a colleague with the laptop works on any other machine until it expires, and st.logout() only clears the local copy. The app-level mitigations available today are shortening the session age in application code and re-checking an allowlist on every rerun. Neither stops a stolen cookie from being used within its window.

DBSC is the web platform's answer to exactly this. The browser generates a key pair in the device's secure hardware at login, and the server issues a short-lived cookie that the browser can only renew by signing a challenge with that key. A copied cookie expires within minutes and cannot be refreshed elsewhere. Chrome shipped it as generally available on Windows in Chrome 146 and is rolling it out on macOS in Chrome 147, and it is a W3C WebAppSec draft. Browsers without support ignore the header and keep working as today, so it degrades cleanly.

Streamlit apps are frequently internal dashboards with real data behind Google or Entra logins, which is the population this protects.

### How?

The change is contained in the Starlette auth layer and needs no frontend work. Sketch:

1. **Registration header.** In the OAuth callback, alongside the existing cookies, send `Secure-Session-Registration` pointing at a new route, with the supported algorithms (ES256, RS256).
2. **Two new routes** next to `/auth/login`, `/auth/logout` and `/auth/callback`:
   - `/auth/dbsc/register`: verifies the browser's signed registration JWT, records the device public key, returns the session config, and sets a short-lived `__Host-` bound cookie.
   - `/auth/dbsc/refresh`: on a missing or expired bound cookie the browser calls this with a signed challenge; the server verifies it against the registered key and reissues the bound cookie.
3. **Stateless key storage.** Streamlit has no server-side session store and runs as one process, so rather than adding one, the device key's thumbprint is written into the existing signed `_streamlit_user` cookie at registration. Refresh verifies the challenge signature against the thumbprint carried in the cookie. Restarts and multiple replicas are then unaffected, matching how the current cookie works.
4. **Websocket check.** The `/_stcore/stream` endpoint, which already decodes the identity cookie on connect, refuses a connection whose identity cookie is bound but whose bound cookie is absent.
5. **Configuration.** A new `[auth]` option, off by default, for example `device_bound_sessions = true`. Requires HTTPS, since `__Host-` cookies are refused otherwise, which is already true of production `st.login()` deployments.

Signature verification can use authlib's JOSE support, which is already a dependency of the auth feature.

One point to verify during implementation: Chrome defers ordinary requests while it refreshes an expired bound cookie, and the behaviour for a WebSocket upgrade is not spelled out in the spec. The frontend fetches `/_stcore/host-config` and `/_stcore/health` over HTTP before opening the stream, which should trigger the refresh first, but this needs a real-browser test.


### Additional Context

- Chrome for Developers, DBSC overview and server integration: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/device-bound-session-credentials
- Chrome 147 macOS rollout: https://scotthelme.co.uk/device-bound-session-credentials-lands-in-chrome-on-macos/

title: Broken relative link in .github/copilot-instructions.md and stale knip ignoreDependencies entries
text:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Two small repository-hygiene defects found while auditing the tree.

**1. Broken relative link in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`**

Line 88 reads:

```markdown
- See [.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md](.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md) for the full debugging guide.
```

The file lives in `.github/`, so the relative link resolves to `.github/.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md`, which does not exist. The real file is at the repository root: `.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md`.

This text is duplicated from `AGENTS.md`, where the same relative link is correct because that file sits at the root — the copy into `.github/` did not adjust the path.

Fix: use `../.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md` (or a root-absolute link).

**2. Stale `ignoreDependencies` entries in `frontend/knip.json`**

`yarn knip` reports three entries that are no longer needed:

```
Configuration hints (3)
@deck.gl/extensions          knip.json  Remove from ignoreDependencies
@deck.gl/widgets             knip.json  Remove from ignoreDependencies
react-responsive-carousel    knip.json  Remove from ignoreDependencies
```

These suppressions now hide nothing, so keeping them only reduces the value of the check.

Fix: drop the three entries.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Open `.github/copilot-instructions.md` on GitHub and click the link on line 88 — it 404s.
2. Run `yarn knip` in `frontend/` and read the "Configuration hints" section.

### Expected Behavior

- The documentation link resolves to the skill file.
- `yarn knip` reports no configuration hints.

### Current Behavior

- The link 404s.
- Three stale hints are reported on every run.
